title: What changes EV vs. equity value
objectives: Answer out loud: Five rapid-fire "what happens to EV and equity value" scenarios.

blocks.body: The test: **does the action change the core business, or just how it's financed?** Financing changes move equity value but not EV. Changes to operations move EV.

blocks.template: Issue $100 of stock, hold the cash → equity value {{1}}, EV {{2}}
Issue $100 of debt, buy $100 of PP&E → EV {{1}}, equity value {{2}}
Pay a $50 dividend → equity value {{1}}, EV {{2}}

blocks.title: Issue $100 of debt and hold the cash — what happens?
blocks.body: Equity unchanged. EV: debt +$100, cash +$100 → unchanged.

blocks.title: Use $100 of cash to buy another company.
blocks.teaser: Equity unchanged (one asset swapped for another).
blocks.body: Equity unchanged (one asset swapped for another). EV up $100: less cash, more operating business.

blocks.prompt: A company uses $100 of cash to buy another company. What happens?
blocks.explanation: Equity value doesn't change (one asset swapped for another). EV rises $100: less cash, more operating business.

blocks.title: Is EV truly independent of capital structure?
blocks.body:
Mostly, but not perfectly. Debt creates interest tax shields (raising value) and distress risk (lowering it). In practice, adding moderate leverage can raise EV a little; too much lowers it.

**Interview answer:** "In theory EV is capital-structure neutral, but tax shields and distress costs mean leverage can shift it at the margins."

blocks.title: If a company's share price rises 10%, what happens?
blocks.body: Equity value up 10%. EV up by the same dollar amount (debt and cash unchanged), which is less than 10% in percentage terms if the company has net debt.
